title: P1 streaming degradation: root cause, on-call notes, and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

P1 incident on 2026-03-02 (13:07 UTC) where hosted-api streaming endpoints experienced a progressive tail-latency degradation culminating in intermittent 502s and truncated streams for ~28 minutes across eu-west-1 and us-east-1. Impact: some customers saw streaming responses stall or return 502 mid-stream; non-streamed (batch/generate) endpoints were largely unaffected.

Detection & initial on-call notes:
- 13:07 UTC: SRE alert (p95 streaming latency > 2s and >5% error rate) fired from datadog monitor streaming-tail-latency-prod.
- 13:09 UTC: On-call (Aisha K.) triaged. Observed: increased per-connection CPU and memory on streaming workers, packet drops at edge (Envoy) counters, and a rise in 502s with client-facing connection resets.
- 13:12 UTC: Scoped to streaming-adapter service (stream-adapter-prod) after correlating traces showing long queue times in adapter accept loop.
- 13:15 UTC: Mitigation path chosen: shift traffic away from problematic pool and enable non-streaming fallback for heavy clients.

Timeline (high level):
- 13:07 Alerting started (p95>2s).
- 13:09 First triage, traces pinned to stream-adapter.
- 13:12 Observed top-of-heap memory growth on stream-adapter workers (heap ~3.8GB -> 7.1GB in 10m on several hosts).
- 13:16 Autoscaler did not trigger fast enough due to >75% CPU threshold and 5m evaluation window.
- 13:18 Manual scale-up of streaming pool started (+40% capacity).
- 13:22 Traffic reroute to warmed fallback pool; temporary decrease in errors.
- 13:35 Full traffic normalized after extra workers reached steady state; investigation continued.

Root cause analysis (current hypothesis):
Primary contributors (combined failure mode):
1) Memory growth in the streaming-adapter process caused long GC/stop-the-world pauses under high-concurrency sessions with large prefix KV caches. The adapter uses a custom ring-buffer for incremental token output; a subtle bug allowed unbounded retention of completed message fragments when clients aborted streams quickly. Over minutes this led to heap growth and increased GC pressure.
2) Autoscaler configuration for the streaming pool (scale-controller-v2) had conservative thresholds: 5m evaluation window and CPU threshold 75%. Under a rapid spike this prevented timely scale-up, so existing workers carried excessive load and GC pauses worsened.
3) Edge/proxy (Envoy) hit socket-level resets when worker threads were unresponsive; Envoy interpreted this as 502s and initiated client disconnects.

Why this only impacted streaming endpoints:
- Streaming workloads keep connections open and manage incremental state (buffers/KV cache) per connection; the bug affects retention semantics of completed fragments only exercised by streaming adapters. Non-streamed generate endpoints are stateless per-request so they didn't accrue retained memory.

Evidence collected:
- Heap profiles from stream-adapter hosts (hosted in S3: s3://redwood-debug/heapdump/2026-03-02/). Marked increases in retained size dominated by ring-buffer and fragment objects.
- Flame graphs showing long GC pause intervals coincident with spike windows (traces available in Datadog trace trace_id: f3e8a2d).
- Autoscaler metrics: backlog queue length rose 3x during 13:10-13:20 but scale events only began at 13:18 due to 5m window.
- Envoy stats showing increased upstream_failure and downstream_rq_5xx for streaming routes.

Immediate mitigations taken (during incident):
- Reroute: traffic partially shifted to separate warm pool with older (stable) binary that had a different buffer implementation (13:18).
- Scale: manual scale up of stream-adapter ASG by +40% (13:18–13:22).
- Fallback: enabled per-customer non-stream fallback (chunked responses) for the largest affected tenants (13:20).
- Monitoring: added short-term alerts for native heap growth >25% in 2m; tightened alert thresholds.

Post-incident actions (short-term):
1) Hotfix (Riley C.) - fix retention bug in ring-buffer to drop completed fragments promptly. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/521 (in review). Target: canary deploy to us-east-1 by 2026-03-07.
2) Autoscaler tuning (Diego M.) - reduce evaluation window to 90s for streaming-pool, and lower CPU threshold to 60% for 30d test window. JIRA: INFRA-3421.
3) Runbook updates (Aisha K./Priya P.) - add streaming-specific memory-growth playbook and checklist for emergency drain and fallback enablement.
4) Post-deploy load test (eng-serving-runtime) - create targeted load test that simulates aborted streams and large KV prefixes to validate memory characteristics.
5) Metric additions - instrument ring-buffer length and completed-fragment retention count as SLO indicators.

Runbook draft (streaming memory pressure / partial outage) - quick steps for on-call:
- Detection: if streaming p95 > 2s OR streaming 5xx > 1% for >2m, begin triage.
- Quick triage checklist:
  * Identify whether errors map to streaming routes only: dd query streaming-route-errors last 10m.
  * Check heap growth on stream-adapter hosts: /monitoring/heap-growth-dashboard.
  * Check accept loop latencies and backlog: dd metric stream-adapter.accept.queue_length.
  * Inspect Envoy upstream/downstream 5xx and reset counters.
- Immediate mitigations (order of ops):
  1) If ring-buffer retention suspected, enable per-tenant non-stream fallback for top affected tenants (via console toggle).
  2) If backlog > threshold and autoscaler hasn't reacted, trigger manual scale up (scale-controller CLI: scale set --pool streaming --replicas +X).
  3) If workers show >50% non-idle GC pause time, consider draining affected nodes (cordon + drain via ASG) and replace with warm nodes.
  4) If Envoy resets persist after worker recovery, rotate envoy listeners or rollback to previous envoy bootstrap config.
- Communication templates: short Slack incident banner, customer email snippet, status page blurb. (templates in confluence link above).

Open follow-ups and owners (owner - deadline):
- Riley Chen - complete ring-buffer retention fix and run unit+integration tests (2026-03-07).
- Diego Martinez - autoscaler config change and rollout plan with rollback (2026-03-10).
- Priya Patel - add new heap/fragment metrics and dashboards; wire alerts (2026-03-09).
- Marcus Lee - create load test simulating aborted streams and >4k prefix KV caching (2026-03-12).
- Aisha Khan - finalize runbook and run a tabletop exercise with on-call rotation (2026-03-16).

Retro notes / lessons learned (informal):
- The incident was the result of compound small failures: a memory retention bug that was rare in single-request workloads + autoscaler config that optimized for cost over rapid elasticity. We should decide where we prefer fast elasticity vs cost for streaming-heavy pools.
- Drift between the new ring-buffer implementation and expectations: the implementation had an optimization for re-use that accidentally kept references. Code review checklist should include explicit mem-retention review for allocator/reuse logic.
- Observability gaps: we lacked a direct metric for 'completed-fragment retention' that would have signaled the specific leak earlier. Instrumentation is now an action item.

Appendix (on-call raw notes):
- 13:10 Aisha: saw spikes on worker-12/13 heap, started tailing logs.
- 13:13 Marcus: heapdump request sent to host-12, grabbed via debug agent.
- 13:17 Riley: looked at ring-buffer implementation; suspicious pattern where fragment list isn't cleared on abort path.
- 13:18 Diego: manual scale invoked; added 6 instances.
- 13:21 Priya: enabled fallback for tenant-acme and tenant-zen. Error rate started dropping.

Files & artifacts collected (s3/dd links):
- s3://redwood-debug/heapdump/2026-03-02/host-12.heap (heapdump)
- Datadog trace: f3e8a2d (13:10-13:22 window)
- Envoy stat snapshot: s3://redwood-debug/envoy/2026-03-02/envoy-stats.json

Notes for final postmortem: once ring-buffer fix is deployed and we complete the autoscaler tuning + load tests, we'll reconvene to convert this draft into a final postmortem with exact RCA language and an incident severity decision note for leadership.

Misc quick links and references:
- Prior similar incident (low-severity): streaming-fragmentation-observed-2025-08-11 (link: confluence) - comparison useful for pattern matching.
- Runbook canonical: confluence.redwood/team-runbooks/streaming-edge-handling

Prepared by: Aisha Khan (on-call)
Collaborators: Marcus Lee, Riley Chen, Diego Martinez, Priya Patel

Status: in_review - feedback welcome on runbook steps and thresholds.
